transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 09:30 - 10:16 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Ananya Rao (Mistral Head of ML), Marcus Li (CTO), David Chen (Data Engineer)

[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick agenda - cost economics, how batching/caching move the needle, and whether Hosted vs Dedicated or Private makes sense for you given the $30k/month ballpark you mentioned.
[00:18] Ananya (Mistral): Yep, thanks Samira. We - hi, hi - we run a bunch of internal analyst workflows, mostly Q&A and summarization. Typical response lengths are 60 to 120 tokens, sometimes up to 400 for long summaries. Our rough monthly volume is around 100M tokens today, expecting to double next quarter.
[00:35] Ethan (Redwood SE): Cool. That token distribution is helpful. Two levers to think about: per-token unit price on Hosted, and for Dedicated how effective batching and KV cache can reduce effective tokens served. Also quantization and model variant selection matter.
[01:02] Marcus (CTO): Quick question - we have a firm budget of about $30k a month for inference now. What realistic throughput and latency are we looking at for that budget?
[01:18] Samira: So rough back-of-envelope: on Hosted, our per-1k-token list price for our curations varies by model family; ballpark example for a 13B-like open model is $0.50 per 1k tokens (note: hypothetical in call), which would be $50k for 100M tokens a month - so that's over your budget. But with batching, caching and smaller model choice you can reduce effective spend a lot.
[01:45] David (Data Eng): Wait, $0.50 per 1k seems high compared to what we saw elsewhere - are you including streaming overhead?
[01:52] Samira: Sorry, let me clarify - that was an example for a high-performance low-latency tier; our lower-cost hosted models and multi-tenant options start closer to $0.15 per 1k tokens. Dedicated reserved capacity is priced differently - it's a combination of a monthly reserved capacity fee (GPU-hours) plus a lower per-token execution overhead.
[02:18] Ethan: To make this practical, we usually run a workload analysis: tokens per request, average response token length, percent of repeated prefixes (for caching potential), and peak concurrency. Those numbers let us model batching gains - for example if your request inter-arrival distribution allows 4-8x batching, you can reduce tokens billed per request by amortizing KV cache and eliminating repeated prefix compute.
[02:45] Ananya: Our prompts are fairly templated - like 3-5 sentence context plus a question. We do a lot of reranking too. I can share prompt samples and histograms.
[03:01] Marcus: What does KV cache savings typically look like? 10%? 30%?
[03:08] Ethan: It varies. For heavily templated prompts with long static context, KV/prefix caching can be 30-60% of token cost savings for subsequent requests. For one-off queries it's lower. With our continuous prefix cache we save the repeated context compute and we only pay for the new tokens. So you might see a big drop if your workflows are interactive or reuse the same context.
[03:38] David: So practically, how do you model for Dedicated? We don't want surprise costs.
[03:44] Samira: Dedicated is simplest to reason about for predictability. It's reserved GPU capacity - you pay a monthly commit (e.g., X GPU-hours for Y GPUs) and that gives you predictable throughput. Unit economics depend on utilization: high utilization drives down per-token costs. We'll share a sizing workbook but example: if you reserve a pool that can handle sustained 300 reqs/sec with average 100 tokens, at high utilization your effective per-1k token cost can drop below hosted list price by 2-4x.
[04:12] Marcus: Are there additional egress or metering addons on Private? We have procurement constraints around data residency.
[04:20] Samira: Private includes optional VPC-only control plane and on-prem installs; pricing is enterprise contract plus platform fee. Egress is typically handled inside your network for Private. We'll add security docs in the follow-up.
[04:34] Ananya: Can you show a worked example? Say 100M tokens, $30k budget.
[04:40] Ethan: Sure - quick numbers: if Hosted list is $0.15 per 1k, 100M tokens = 100,000 k tokens * $0.15 = $15,000 - actually that fits. But if your model variant is larger or latency SLO pushes you to high-perf tier, costs climb. More important is effective tokens billed after caching.
[05:02] Samira: Right. Another example: if you adopt Dedicated and through batching + caching reduce compute equivalent to 40% fewer tokens, your net billed compute might be 60M tokens equivalent. If your Dedicated amortized cost (including GPU reservation) translates to an equivalent of $0.08 per 1k effective tokens at 75% utilization, 60M tokens ~ $4,800. Add platform and support and you're well below $30k. But the dedicated commitment is the risk - if utilization is low it doesn't pay.
[05:35] Marcus: So utilization smoothing is key. How flexible is scaling? Can we burst?
[05:41] Samira: Dedicated can be configured with burst capacity into hosted pools. Autoscaling policies let you keep a reserved baseline and burst to hosted in overflow. That hybrid approach helps control commit size while keeping reliability.
[06:00] Ananya: What's the timeline to get a Dedicated pool up? We have procurement timelines but want to pilot quickly.
[06:07] Ethan: Typical pilot we do is 2-4 weeks: we run a benchmark harness on your prompts, validate latency, and then recommend a committed capacity. Private on-prem takes longer due to installation. Hosted sample tests can start in days.
[06:24] David: About batching - our latency SLO is ~300ms p95 for interactive flows. Does batching destroy that?
[06:31] Ethan: Not necessarily. Continuous batching and dynamic batching are tuned for latency-sensitive workloads; you can set latency SLOs and we cap batch windows. In many cases you get 2-3x batching without breaking 300ms p95 depending on request concurrency. If strict single-digit-ms latency is required, batching potential reduces.
[06:55] Marcus: Any hidden costs like tokenization differences or special token counting?
[07:00] Samira: We bill on normalized token counts using our tokenizer; there can be small deltas vs other vendors. We'll surface token histograms so you can reconcile. Also embeddings and long-context costs are separate line items, we'll show that in the spreadsheet.
[07:18] Ananya: Can you explain how quantization helps on Dedicated?
[07:23] Ethan: Yes. Quantized model execution reduces GPU memory footprint and can increase throughput. On some architectures it can reduce latency and cost per token without significant quality regression. We recommend running evals on your prompts. We'll include suggested quantization profiles; some customers run 4-bit or 8-bit depending on model.
[07:42] David: We do reranking (top-K) a lot - how does that affect cost?
[07:47] Ethan: Reranking multiplies request count or compute; if you can do it server-side with cached embeddings or condensed prompts it helps. We'll model reranking separately; it can look like N times a base request.
[08:03] Marcus: Ok sounds good. Can you quantify savings if we move templated flows that reuse context to use prefix caching?
[08:10] Samira: Example: if 60% of each request is the same 512-token prompt and only 20 tokens change, with prefix caching you'd only generate and bill the new tokens in many cases after warm-up. So effective billed tokens can drop 4-5x for those flows. Real savings depend on cache hit rate and TTLs.
[08:34] Ananya: Do you support per-route SLOs and different model pinning? We want some routes on smaller cheaper models and a few high-accuracy routes on larger models.
[08:40] Samira: Yes, per-route model pinning and routing policies are standard. You can route by cost, latency, or tenant, and fallback to cheaper variants automatically.
[08:50] David: If we wanted to experiment with Dedicated for, say, 25% of traffic, how do you recommend splitting and measuring?
[08:57] Ethan: Start with a canary: route a subset of traffic through Dedicated and measure latency and token per request delta, then scale commit size. We'll provide dashboards for per-route cost and token breakdowns.
[09:12] Marcus: Any contract examples for Dedicated - commitment lengths, cancellation?
[09:18] Samira: Usually 3-12 month commitments; we can do monthly but with higher rate. We'll include options in the pricing doc.
[09:28] Ananya: Back to budget - if our budget is fixed at $30k, but expected tokens grow to 200M next quarter, what's the best path?
[09:36] Samira: Two pragmatic routes: 1) Host multi-tenant for baseline and use batching and model distillation to keep per-token cost low while you grow; 2) Start with a small Dedicated commit for heavy-heavy flows that benefit from caching and burst-host for the rest. We'll run a modeled projection and show which hybrid hits $30k at your anticipated growth.
[09:56] David: We'll share token histograms and example prompts after this.
[10:00] Ethan: Great. On the benchmarking side, we'll need a sample corpus and target concurrency numbers. We'll run both hosted and a dedicated-like local run to estimate batch wins.
[10:10] Marcus: One last thing - procurement asks for an example invoice and an SLA.
[10:15] Samira: We'll include sample contract terms and SLA summary in the follow-up.
[10:20] Ananya: Cool, thanks.
[10:22] Samira: Recap of next steps - Samira send pricing spreadsheet and contract examples; Ethan run micro-bench; Mistral share prompts and histograms; schedule dedicated sizing call. Thanks everyone.
[10:35] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcript had small name mislabels; technical terms like KV cache sometimes transcribed as "K-V cache" or "K V cache". There are some filler words and cross-talk preserved.
